newsitem.title: USA: Briton dies after fall from Alaska's Mt. McKinley.
newsitem.headline: Briton dies after fall from Alaska's Mt. McKinley.

text.p: The first climber to be to killed this year on Alaska's Mount McKinley was Mark Trevillyan of Aldershot in Britain, officials said on Saturday.

National Park Service spokesman John Quinley said Trevillyan's body remained on the Messner Couloir, a steep gully on the 20,320-foot (6,194-metre) peak because conditions were too windy for rangers to retrieve it.
Trevillyan's companion, to whom he was roped, was injured in fall, originally estimated at 500 feet (15-metre) but officials said later they could not tell exactly how far they fell.
Paul Holmes, 27, of London, was evacuated by helicopter on Saturday from the mountain's 14,200-foot (4,300-metre) ranger camp, then flown to an Anchorage hospital, Quinley said.

Trevillyan, whose age was not released, and Holmes became lost in a whiteout after reaching the peak's summit late on Thursday. Holmes was knocked temporarily unconsious in the fall; when he regained consciousness, he found his dead companion on top of him. Holmes was rescued on Friday morning by another climber.

Trevillyan and Holmes had been in a four-man British climbing party. Members were fairly accomplished mountaineers, "but were lacking any cold winter experience or other Alaska high-altitude experience," Quinley said. "They had been on high-altitude places, but in milder conditions."
Still camped out on the mountain Saturday were their companions, Martin Kitson, 30, of Church Crookum, and Matthew Yorke, 25, of Damerham, Quinley said.
Until Trevillyan's death, the 1997 McKinley climbing season had been one of the safest on record. The climbing season runs from late April to mid-July.
